{"id":"MM-377","title":"Wallet-driven per-account repo signing-key rotation","description":"## Problem

A per-account repo signing key (the PDS-held P-256 key at `verificationMethods.atproto` + `rotationKeys[1]`, which signs every repo commit — ADR-0004) currently cannot be rotated to a **fresh value**. Re-wrapping under a new KEK (<issue id="7bf34d8c-b8d9-4143-9cde-014d62e6515d" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-375/master-key-kek-re-wrap-rotation-tooling">MM-375</issue>) preserves the same key material; it does nothing if the plaintext repo key itself is compromised (attacker had KEK + DB) or lost (KEK gone → key undecryptable forever). In both cases the only real fix is issuing a *new* repo key and repointing the DID document at it — which requires a PLC operation.

## Why the PDS can't do this unilaterally

The PDS would have to sign the rotation op with a current rotation key. Its own key is `rotationKeys[1]` — the exact key being distrusted in a compromise, and undecryptable in a loss. The **wallet holds** `rotationKeys[0]`, which outranks the PDS key and is the sovereign controller (ADR-0001, `identity-and-key-custody.md`). So repo-key rotation is inherently a **wallet-driven, per-account** flow, reusing the existing recovery/override machinery (`apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/recovery.rs`, `plc_monitor.rs`).

## Proposed flow (per account)

1. **PDS generates a fresh repo signing key** (P-256), stores it encrypted (new `signing_keys` row for the DID — `get_signing_key_by_did` already selects newest by `created_at`, so the write path picks up the new key once present).
2. **PDS exposes the new** `verificationMethods.atproto` **(+** `rotationKeys[1]`**)** for the wallet to include in a rotation op — likely an extension of `getRecommendedDidCredentials` or a dedicated endpoint.
3. **Wallet signs the PLC rotation op** with the device key (`rotationKeys[0]`), chaining on the current head, and submits to [plc.directory](<http://plc.directory>) (`build_did_plc_rotation_op` already exists in the crypto crate).
4. **PDS begins signing commits with the new key** once the DID doc update is observed; the old key row can be retired.
5. Firehose `#identity` frame so relays re-resolve.

## Open questions

* Ordering/atomicity between the PDS starting to sign with the new key and the DID doc actually updating on [plc.directory](<http://plc.directory>) (avoid a window where commits are signed by a key not yet in the doc). Likely: keep signing with old key until the new `verificationMethods.atproto` is live, then cut over.
* Batch/operator-initiated variant for mass rotation (compromise scenario) vs. single-account user-initiated. Mass rotation still needs each wallet to sign — surface as a prompt/queue in Obsign?
* Relationship to `recovery.rs` (tamper counter-op) — this is a *sibling* flow (rotate a distrusted-but-not-tampered key), not the same code path, but shares op-building and submission.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A single account can rotate its repo signing key end-to-end: fresh key generated, DID doc repointed via wallet-signed PLC op, commits signed by the new key, relays re-resolve.
- [ ] No window where a commit is signed by a key absent from the DID doc.
- [ ] Old key material retired after cutover.
- [ ] Documented as the recovery mechanism referenced by the compromise/loss runbook (related issue).

## Notes

Keep threat-model prose in Linear, not the public repo, per maintainer preference. This is the load-bearing piece of both the compromise and loss recovery stories — <issue id="7bf34d8c-b8d9-4143-9cde-014d62e6515d" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-375/master-key-kek-re-wrap-rotation-tooling">MM-375</issue> (re-wrap) is necessary hygiene but insufficient on its own.","priority":{"value":3,"name":"Medium"},"url":"https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-377/wallet-driven-per-account-repo-signing-key-rotation","gitBranchName":"malpercio/mm-377-wallet-driven-per-account-repo-signing-key-rotation","createdAt":"2026-07-15T17:01:45.606Z","updatedAt":"2026-07-15T17:01:45.606Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"slaType":"all","status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":["Security","Wave 3: Key Sovereignty"],"attachments":[],"documents":[],"stateHistory":[{"state":{"id":"907302ec-02e8-46f0-985c-f57a0960720f","name":"Backlog","type":"backlog"},"startedAt":"2026-07-15T17:01:45.606Z","endedAt":null}],"createdBy":"Malpercio","createdById":"5af222b1-08a6-485f-b6e6-26ff3fcff509","project":"ezpds","projectId":"2b0ca2e9-cd15-4ab2-8a55-1efad70eb8a1","team":"Mal's Machinations","teamId":"9278a20f-995f-49ab-b09d-a340fdcaea72"}

content.thinking:
The three issues are solid and actually go beyond what I'd initially planned—they're grounded in real code details like table names, migration versions, and specific failure points rather than just abstract concepts. Now I need to assess whether they match expectations and identify any gaps or adjustments I'd want to make.

Checking against my mental model: all eight key areas are covered—the four secret families, the re-wrap versus rotate distinction, per-account rotation requiring wallet PLC operations, the loss versus compromise runbook, blast radius including admin tokens and SMTP, KEK backup discipline, no-downtime atomicity, and the kek_version marker for detecting half-applied states. But here's the critical gap: these issues are framed as *future tooling to build*, when in reality this is a *current compromise event happening today*—the production KEK has already been exposed.

The actual incident is that the production KEK value was copied into staging's config, which sits on the same Railway account. Since staging has its own database and there's no external attacker involved, this is closer to a "key alone" exposure rather than a full compromise. The blast radius is limited to whoever can access staging's config—in this case, just the person who accidentally exposed it on a solo hobby project.

The immediate response is straightforward: remove the production key from staging (already done, with staging now using its own recovered key) and optionally rotate the production KEK as a hygiene measure once the tooling exists. Since there's no external compromise and no immediate way to rotate without MM-375, it's reasonable to accept the risk and focus on building that tooling first.

The gap here is that the issues capture the build work but don't address what to do about the exposure that just happened without any tooling in place. MM-376 would be the runbook for this, but it depends on MM-375 existing first. For the immediate event with no tooling available, the only real action is containment—which has already been done.

The key point to communicate clearly: this incident is low-severity given the constraints, so mal shouldn't feel pressured into an emergency production rotation with no proper tooling. MM-375 and MM-376 are the proper follow-ups, and that's where the effort should go.

There's a subtle tension in the prioritization though — MM-377 is marked Medium but it's actually the load-bearing piece for the compromise recovery path. The runbook (MM-376, High) can't be executed without it, and since repo key rotation is the catastrophic part of any real compromise, there's an argument that MM-377 should be elevated to High as well. Worth flagging, though it's a minor point. I should also check whether these issues have formal blocking links in Linear or if they're just referenced in prose — if not, I could add those dependency relations to keep them properly sequenced.

The runbook itself focuses on response but doesn't address detection — how would you even know the KEK was exposed in the first place? For an accidental leak it's obvious, but against an actual attacker there's no mention of monitoring or alerting (like watching for the env var in logs or auditing Railway access). On a hobby plan without audit logs, detection becomes pretty limited, though that might be out of scope here.

I'm also wondering about the Shamir escrow share stored on the relay — MM-375 lists the tables that need re-wrapping, but does that include the escrow share? If the relay holds a KEK-wrapped Shamir share, that needs to be part of the rotation too. Checking the storage implementation in the crates to see if that escrow share is actually KEK-encrypted.

input.description:
## Purpose

Write and keep (in Linear / an internal location, **not** the public repo) the operator runbook for two distinct `EZPDS_SIGNING_KEY_MASTER_KEY` disaster scenarios. Today there is no documented procedure and no tooling; this issue captures the procedure and the decisions behind it. Depends on the re-wrap tool (MM-375) and the wallet-driven repo-key rotation flow (MM-377) for the actual mechanics.

## Two scenarios, deliberately separated

### 1. KEK *lost* (not exposed)

The server won't boot if encrypted material exists and the key is gone (`decode_oauth_signing_key` and the JWT/Iroh loaders hard-error). Recovery:

* **OAuth key / JWT secret / Iroh key** — delete their single rows; `load_or_create_*` re-mints under a fresh KEK on next boot. Cost: all sessions invalidated (users re-auth), node id changes (devices re-resolve).
* **Per-account repo signing keys** — **permanently undecryptable.** The server can no longer sign commits under the published `verificationMethods.atproto`. Only fix is the wallet-driven per-account repo-key rotation (MM-377).
* **Implication to document:** a lost KEK is nearly as catastrophic as a compromised one, *because of the repo keys*. → **The KEK must be backed up as carefully as the DB, and stored separately from it** (backing them up together defeats the encryption). Add this to deploy guidance. Note the escrow Shamir shares (`accounts.recovery_share`) currently **survive** a KEK loss because they are stored plaintext — a property that KEK-wrapping them (see the open decision below) would remove, folding escrow into the KEK-loss blast radius.

### 2. KEK *compromised* (assume DB also exposed)

Treat every KEK-wrapped secret as plaintext-known to the attacker.

* **Cheap secrets** — drop `oauth_signing_key` / `jwt_signing_secret` / `iroh_identity`, re-mint under a new KEK (via MM-375 re-wrap for the surviving repo blobs + row-drop for these).
* **Repo keys** — cannot be rotated server-side cleanly: the key the PDS would sign a rotation op with (`rotationKeys[1]`) is itself the compromised key. Recovery is **wallet-driven and per-account**: the user's wallet holds `rotationKeys[0]`, which outranks the PDS key, and signs a PLC op rotating `verificationMethods.atproto` + `rotationKeys[1]` to a fresh PDS-generated key (leverages the existing `recovery.rs` / `plc_monitor.rs` custody capabilities; see MM-377). Prioritize active accounts.
* **Escrow Shamir shares** — `accounts.recovery_share` (Share 2 of each user's 2-of-3 recovery split, V010) is stored **base32 plaintext, not KEK-wrapped**, so a DB dump exposes it directly. The 2-of-3 threshold means one share reconstructs nothing (Shamir is information-theoretically secure at a single share), so this stays **sub-threshold** — the recovery secret is not reconstructable from Share 2 alone. But it erodes the margin and belongs in the blast-radius accounting. **Open decision:** whether to KEK-wrap this share at rest (see Deliverables) — wrapping upgrades a *DB-only* leak (no env-var exposure) from one-share-exposed to zero, at the cost of coupling escrow recovery to KEK availability.
* **Env blast radius** — whatever exposed the KEK (leaked Railway vars / dashboard access) almost certainly exposed `admin_token`, SMTP/Mailtrap tokens too. The runbook must rotate **all** env-var secrets, not just the KEK. `admin_token` is the urgent one (break-glass bearer credential).

## Deliverables

- [ ] Internal runbook covering both scenarios with concrete step ordering.
- [ ] Deploy guidance: KEK backup discipline (separate from DB backup), and where operators actually store it.
- [ ] Cross-reference the re-wrap tool (MM-375) and repo-key rotation flow (MM-377).
- [ ] Decide whether to KEK-wrap `accounts.recovery_share` at rest (defense-in-depth for DB-only leaks vs. coupling escrow to KEK availability) — track the decision in a dedicated issue.
- [ ] Decide where the internal runbook lives (Linear doc vs. private ops repo) — must stay out of the public repo.

## Context (reference, keep private)

Custody model: `docs/architecture/identity-and-key-custody.md`, ADR-0001 (client-held rotation key), ADR-0004 (PDS-signed repo commits). The wallet-at-`rotationKeys[0]` sovereignty is what makes repo-key recovery possible without the old PDS's cooperation — and what makes it inherently distributed rather than a single server operation.

{"id":"MM-377","title":"Wallet-driven per-account repo signing-key rotation","description":"## Problem

A per-account repo signing key (the PDS-held P-256 key at `verificationMethods.atproto` + `rotationKeys[1]`, which signs every repo commit — ADR-0004) currently cannot be rotated to a **fresh value**. Re-wrapping under a new KEK (<issue id="7bf34d8c-b8d9-4143-9cde-014d62e6515d" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-375/master-key-kek-re-wrap-rotation-tooling">MM-375</issue>) preserves the same key material; it does nothing if the plaintext repo key itself is compromised (attacker had KEK + DB) or lost (KEK gone → key undecryptable forever). In both cases the only real fix is issuing a *new* repo key and repointing the DID document at it — which requires a PLC operation.

## Why the PDS can't do this unilaterally

The PDS would have to sign the rotation op with a current rotation key. Its own key is `rotationKeys[1]` — the exact key being distrusted in a compromise, and undecryptable in a loss. The **wallet holds** `rotationKeys[0]`, which outranks the PDS key and is the sovereign controller (ADR-0001, `identity-and-key-custody.md`). So repo-key rotation is inherently a **wallet-driven, per-account** flow, reusing the existing recovery/override machinery (`apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/recovery.rs`, `plc_monitor.rs`).

## Proposed flow (per account)

1. **PDS generates a fresh repo signing key** (P-256), stores it encrypted (new `signing_keys` row for the DID — `get_signing_key_by_did` already selects newest by `created_at`, so the write path picks up the new key once present).
2. **PDS exposes the new** `verificationMethods.atproto` **(+** `rotationKeys[1]`**)** for the wallet to include in a rotation op — likely an extension of `getRecommendedDidCredentials` or a dedicated endpoint.
3. **Wallet signs the PLC rotation op** with the device key (`rotationKeys[0]`), chaining on the current head, and submits to [plc.directory](<http://plc.directory>) (`build_did_plc_rotation_op` already exists in the crypto crate).
4. **PDS begins signing commits with the new key** once the DID doc update is observed; the old key row can be retired.
5. Firehose `#identity` frame so relays re-resolve.

## Open questions

* Ordering/atomicity between the PDS starting to sign with the new key and the DID doc actually updating on [plc.directory](<http://plc.directory>) (avoid a window where commits are signed by a key not yet in the doc). Likely: keep signing with old key until the new `verificationMethods.atproto` is live, then cut over.
* Batch/operator-initiated variant for mass rotation (compromise scenario) vs. single-account user-initiated. Mass rotation still needs each wallet to sign — surface as a prompt/queue in Obsign?
* Relationship to `recovery.rs` (tamper counter-op) — this is a *sibling* flow (rotate a distrusted-but-not-tampered key), not the same code path, but shares op-building and submission.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A single account can rotate its repo signing key end-to-end: fresh key generated, DID doc repointed via wallet-signed PLC op, commits signed by the new key, relays re-resolve.
- [ ] No window where a commit is signed by a key absent from the DID doc.
- [ ] Old key material retired after cutover.
- [ ] Documented as the recovery mechanism referenced by the compromise/loss runbook (related issue).

## Notes

Keep threat-model prose in Linear, not the public repo, per maintainer preference. This is the load-bearing piece of both the compromise and loss recovery stories — <issue id="7bf34d8c-b8d9-4143-9cde-014d62e6515d" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-375/master-key-kek-re-wrap-rotation-tooling">MM-375</issue> (re-wrap) is necessary hygiene but insufficient on its own.","priority":{"value":2,"name":"High"},"url":"https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-377/wallet-driven-per-account-repo-signing-key-rotation","gitBranchName":"malpercio/mm-377-wallet-driven-per-account-repo-signing-key-rotation","createdAt":"2026-07-15T17:01:45.606Z","updatedAt":"2026-07-15T20:27:06.434Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"slaType":"all","status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":["Security","Wave 3: Key Sovereignty"],"attachments":[],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Malpercio","createdById":"5af222b1-08a6-485f-b6e6-26ff3fcff509","project":"ezpds","projectId":"2b0ca2e9-cd15-4ab2-8a55-1efad70eb8a1","team":"Mal's Machinations","teamId":"9278a20f-995f-49ab-b09d-a340fdcaea72"}

## Should we KEK-wrap the escrow share? My take: **yes, worth doing — but as a deliberate, tracked decision, and contingent on the KEK-backup discipline landing.**

Here's the reasoning, threat model by threat model:

| Exposure | Plaintext (today) | KEK-wrapped |
|---|---|---|
| **DB-only leak** (Litestream backup, volume snapshot, SQLi read — *no* env vars) | Share 2 exposed (1 of 3) | **0 of 3** exposed |
| **Full compromise** (KEK + DB, MM-376 scenario 2) | Share 2 exposed | Share 2 exposed (attacker has the KEK) — **no gain** |
| **KEK loss** | shares **survive** (still recoverable) | shares become **undecryptable** — folded into the KEK-loss blast radius |

**The case for wrapping:** the KEK and the DB have *different* exposure surfaces — the KEK is a Railway env var; the DB is a Litestream backup / volume. A DB dump without the env vars is the single most common real-world leak, and that's exactly the case where wrapping helps: it takes you from "one share of every user leaked" to "nothing useful leaked." That's the textbook rationale for encryption-at-rest, and it restores the full 2-of-3 margin under a DB-only compromise.

**The case against / the cost:** Shamir 2-of-3 is *information-theoretically* secure at a single share — one share is provably zero information about the secret. So plaintext storage wasn't an oversight; it was a defensible choice resting on that guarantee. Wrapping adds a *computationally*-secure outer layer on top of an already-sub-threshold value — real defense-in-depth, but margin, not a hole-fix. The genuine downside is **availability coupling**: the escrow share exists as a *recovery* mechanism, and wrapping it means recovery now depends on the KEK being available — you'd be protecting the recovery share with the very key whose loss it partly exists to survive. Today a KEK loss doesn't destroy escrow; wrapping would add escrow to that blast radius.

**Why the cost is acceptable:** MM-376 is *already* establishing "the KEK must be backed up as carefully as the DB, stored separately." Once that discipline is real, "irrecoverable KEK loss" stops being a live risk — and the availability objection largely dissolves. So the two work items compose: land the KEK-backup discipline, then wrapping the escrow share is nearly free upside.

**Implementation note (cheap):** the stored share is 52-char base32 = **exactly 32 bytes**, which is the precise shape `crypto::encrypt_private_key` already takes (`&[u8; 32]` plaintext). So it's close to a drop-in reuse — one migration to widen `accounts.recovery_share` to hold the 80-char wrapped blob, plus a re-wrap pass for existing rows (which MM-375's tool would then also need to cover — making the escrow share a *fifth* re-wrap family after all, once wrapped).

Net: I'd do it, sequenced **after** the KEK-backup discipline, and note that wrapping promotes the escrow share into MM-375's re-wrap scope.

Want me to file the dedicated issue for it (the MM-376 deliverable references one) — "KEK-wrap the escrow Shamir share at rest," Security / Wave 7, blocked-by MM-376's backup-discipline decision, and noting the MM-375 re-wrap coupling? I'll create it on your go.

input.title: KEK-wrap the escrow Shamir share (accounts.recovery_share) at rest
input.description:
## Problem

`accounts.recovery_share` (Share 2 of each user's 2-of-3 Shamir recovery split, added in V010) is stored **base32 plaintext**, not KEK-wrapped. Every other long-lived server-held secret (OAuth ES256 key, JWT HS256 secret, Iroh Ed25519 key, per-account repo signing keys) is wrapped by `EZPDS_SIGNING_KEY_MASTER_KEY` via `crypto::encrypt_private_key`; the escrow share is the one exception. Surfaced while auditing the KEK blast radius for MM-376.

A DB-only leak (Litestream backup, volume snapshot, SQL read) with **no** env-var exposure therefore hands the attacker every account's Share 2 in the clear.

## Why this is not a live hole (today's posture is defensible)

Shamir 2-of-3 is **information-theoretically** secure at a single share: one share is provably zero information about the recovery secret. Storing Share 2 plaintext was a reasoned choice, not an oversight — a DB-only leak stays **sub-threshold** (Share 2 alone reconstructs nothing; the attacker still needs Share 1 from iCloud Keychain or Share 3 from the user's manual backup). This issue is **defense-in-depth margin**, not a break-glass fix. Hence Medium.

## Threat analysis

| Exposure | Plaintext (today) | KEK-wrapped |
| -- | -- | -- |
